trace.result_text:
[Septoria_brown_spot] Symptoms:
Septoria brown spot is the most common foliar disease of soybean, developing soon after planting and typically present throughout the growing season. Symptoms are typically mild during the vegetative stages and progress upward from lower leaves during grain fill. Infected young plants exhibit small, irregularly shaped, dark brown lesions on the unifoliate leaves. Lesions on later leaves are small and found on both leaf surfaces, often growing larger and forming irregularly shaped blotches. Infected leaves quickly turn yellow and drop. The disease starts in the lower canopy, and if conditions remain favorable, it will progress to the upper canopy, potentially leading to yield losses that depend on how far up the canopy the disease progresses during grain fill. The key difference between Septoria brown spot and Bacterial blight is that the latter shows tattering of leaf tissues, while Septoria does not. | Often confused with: Brown_Stem_Rot

[Soybean_rust] Symptoms:
Soybean rust (Phakopsora pachyrhizi) symptoms commonly appear on lower leaves after flowering. Initially, lesions form as small gray spots that transition to tan or reddish-brown. These lesions are scattered and appear in yellow areas, becoming translucent when held up to the sun. Mature lesions may contain numerous small pustules, typically found on lower leaf surfaces. The disease is favored by cool, wet conditions or high humidity, and dense canopies provide ideal conditions for its development. The symptoms can be distinguished from similar diseases like bacterial blight and Septoria brown spot by the specific lesion coloration and structure. Compared to Septoria brown spot, Soybean rust tends to show more pronounced yellowing around the lesions. | Often confused with: Soybean_Cyst_Nematode | Often confused with: Soybean_Dwarf_Mosaic_Virus | Often confused with: Soybean_Vein_necrosis_virus

[Frogeye_leaf_spot] Symptoms:
Frogeye leaf spot can cause significant yield loss when widespread within a field. Leaf lesions are small, irregular to circular in shape, and gray with reddish-brown borders. Most commonly occurring on the upper leaf surface, lesions start as dark, water-soaked spots that vary in size. As lesions age, the central area becomes gray to light brown with dark red-brown margins. In severe cases, the disease can cause premature leaf drop and will spread to stems and pods. The fungus survives in infested crop residue and infected seed, and warm, humid weather promotes spore production, infection, and disease development. | Often confused with: Phyllosticta_leaf_spot
